# How to Animate an SVG with Motion | Media Manipulator Tutorial

- Route: `/tutorials/motion`
- Kind: `page`
- Category: `tutorials`

## Summary

Step-by-step Motion tutorial: import an SVG, animate it with keyframes, shape the timing with easing and holds, then export animated SVG, Lottie, code or GIF.

## Details

How to animate an SVG with Aperture
Aperture turns a static SVG into an animation without writing code. You work with layers and a keyframe timeline, like a motion design app, and export the result as an animated SVG, a Lottie file, a React component, a JavaScript or TypeScript module, a Flutter widget or a GIF. This guide goes from an empty canvas to a finished export in five steps.
1. Import an SVG or start from scratch
Open Aperture from its tool page. The editor opens full screen with a blank 512 × 512 canvas. Choose Import to bring in your artwork, or draw directly on the canvas.
SVG files become a layer tree: groups, paths, rectangles, ellipses, lines, polygons, text, images, gradients, masks and clip paths are all editable. Select a layer in the Layers panel or on the canvas, and rename, group, lock or hide it.
Lottie JSON files are imported with their keyframes, so you can edit an existing animation. Anything the editor cannot represent is listed after the import instead of being dropped silently.
To draw from scratch, use the Rectangle, Ellipse, Line, Pen and Text tools. Edit nodes lets you reshape any path point by point.
Imports are cleaned on the way in: scripts, event handlers and links to outside files are removed and listed, so an SVG from the web cannot run code in the editor or in your exports.
2. Animate with keyframes
The timeline at the bottom of the editor shows one row per layer and one track per animated property. Aperture uses the playhead to decide where a change goes.
Drag the playhead (or click the time ruler) to the moment the change should happen. Space plays and pauses, Home and End jump to the start and end.
With a layer selected, use Animate on a property in the inspector to give it a track, then change the value. Each change at a new time adds a keyframe; changing an animated property later edits the keyframe at the playhead.
Turn on Auto-key to record every change you make on the canvas or in the inspector as a keyframe, which is fastest for rough blocking.
The Animate panel adds whole effects in one step: Draw on (the stroke draws itself), Motion path (the layer travels along a path), Morph (one shape becomes another), Gradient, Mask/Clip and Blur. Each one is a single undo step.
3. Shape the timing with easing and holds
Easing decides how a value travels between two keyframes. Select one or more keyframes on the timeline and pick an easing in the Easing panel; it applies to the segment that starts at each selected keyframe.
Linear, Ease in, Ease out and Ease in-out cover most motion. Ease out suits things arriving; ease in suits things leaving.
Curve opens a cubic-bezier editor with two handles, for overshoot-free custom timing that matches CSS cubic-bezier() exactly.
Hold keeps the value unchanged until the next keyframe, then jumps. Use it for blinking, frame-by-frame swaps or a colour that changes instantly.
Set a play range to loop just the part you are working on, and turn Loop off if the animation should play once.
4. Export your animation
Choose Export to open the export dialog. Every export is made in your browser and downloaded straight away; your artwork is not uploaded. Static SVG (the frame at the playhead) is always free. Animated formats count toward your plan's daily Aperture allowance, which the dialog shows before you export, and formats your plan does not include are marked with a lock and a link to the plans.
5. Pick the right format
The best format depends on where the animation will play.
Animated SVG is one file that plays without any library, ideal for websites. It uses pure CSS when it can; shape morphs, moving gradient stops and blur need a small embedded script (anime.js, MIT licence), and scripts do not run when the SVG is placed in an tag.
Lottie JSON plays in lottie-web and the iOS, Android and Flutter Lottie players. The dialog lists anything Lottie cannot carry, such as filters or text.
React (.tsx), JavaScript and TypeScript exports give you a component or module with play, pause and seek, ready to drop into an app.
The Flutter export is a native flutter_svg widget when the animation only moves, fades and recolours, and a WebView player for everything else.
GIF plays everywhere, including chat and email, with one global palette that keeps flat vector colours exact. GIF and video exports follow your plan's size and length limits.
Saving your work
Aperture saves a draft in this browser as you work, so a closed tab or a crash does not lose your changes. Without an account, projects live only in this browser. When you are signed in, Save to account stores the project on our servers; after that it autosaves, opens on any device and appears on your Account page, where you can delete it.
